ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's foreign policy is currently challenged by internal ethnic politics and political patronage, which hinder its ability to effectively represent national interests abroad. The government faces criticism for appointing diplomats based on political connections rather than merit, raising concerns about professionalism and competence within its diplomatic corps. Recent appointments include individuals with questionable backgrounds, prompting doubts about the criteria used for selection. This practice risks creating a diplomatic service filled with "Innocents Abroad," lacking the necessary skills in international relations, law, and negotiation. Additionally, corruption and nepotism within public institutions further compromise Ethiopia's diplomatic integrity. As a strategically significant nation, Ethiopia must prioritize a coherent foreign policy and professional diplomatic representation to navigate complex international relationships, particularly regarding issues like the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and regional tensions. Without addressing these internal challenges, Ethiopia risks damaging its international reputation and undermining its long-term strategic interests.

ethiopia.title: Power Without Transparency - Who Holds Ethiopia's Media Regulator Accountable When It Silences the Press?
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Power Without Transparency - Who Holds Ethiopia's Media Regulator Accountable When It Silences the Press? - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Power Without Transparency - Who Holds Ethiopia's Media Regulator Accountable When It Silences the Press? 18 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion On 2 November 2026, the Ethiopian Media Authority (EMA) announced the indefinite suspension of the registration certificate of Media and Communication Center PLC, the publisher of the Amharic-language Reporter and the English-language The Reporter, and their digital platforms. One of Ethiopia's longest-established independent media organizations was brought to a halt. That raises a question bigger than one publisher: who holds the media regulator accountable when it uses its power to silence an entire outlet? The EMA says it monitored the publisher for more than a year, raised its concerns with the owner and editors, and gave a final warning before acting. It accuses the organization of repeatedly publishing distorted, unbalanced, or unverified material that, in its words, harmed national interests, investment, tourism, and diplomacy. Those are the Authority's allegations. They are not findings the public can check for itself, because so little has been released. No media organization is above the law. Journalists must verify facts, correct their errors, and respect professional standards. But the state is not above accountability either. When a public authority suspends a publisher indefinitely, it owes the public the legal basis, the evidence, and the reasoning. The bigger the impact of a restriction, the stronger the public's interest in knowing why it was imposed. Regulatory decision with political consequences Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn This is not just an administrative matter. The Reporter has covered politics, economic policy, regional affairs, and social developments for readers in Amharic and English. Human Rights Watch describes it as one of Ethiopia's oldest media institutions and the country's last privately owned Amharic newspaper. According to Addis Standard , the suspension covers its print and broadcast operations, including its digital platforms. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the decision unjustified and said the accusations are vague and do not name the content concerned. When an established independent publisher disappears from public debate, the loss reaches far beyond its owners and staff. Readers lose a source of reporting and analysis. Officials face fewer independent questions. Citizens have fewer ways to compare different accounts of events and policy. That is why this suspension has to be judged not only as a regulatory act but also as a question of political accountability and of the balance between the state and society. A regulator that demands accountability from the press must be prepared to face accountability itself." None of this proves, on its own, that the EMA acted on political instructions. But the timing and the pattern raise questions the Authority should answer. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reports that The Reporter published an editorial on 31 October criticizing the authorities for treating independent reporting as a national security threat. Two days later it was suspended. Human Rights Watch (HRW) places the decision within a widening crackdown on independent journalism and civic space and notes that since 2025 the authorities have banned numerous media outlets, deported foreign correspondents, and arrested journalists, including from The Reporter itself. The EMA also revoked the registration of Addis Standard's publisher in February, a decision the publisher is challenging in court . Timing and pattern are not proof of motive. Still, when a state regulator sanctions an outlet shortly after it criticizes the state, the public is entitled to ask whether the decision was driven by regulatory standards or by political convenience. Where the state regulates the very institutions that scrutinize it, public confidence depends on visible safeguards against arbitrary or selective use of power. The public has not been shown the case The Authority's public explanation sets out broad categories of concern, but it fails to identify the specific articles or broadcasts on which the allegations rest. It gives no publication dates, does not reproduce the material at issue, and does not explain how each item broke a legal provision. Without those details, the public cannot tell whether the dispute is about demonstrable factual errors, missing context, professional lapses, or simply reporting that is critical of those in power. The lack of an end date makes this worse. As Addis Standard reported , the EMA said the suspension will stay in force until the publisher's legal and professional obligations are fully met and implemented. If the Authority does not say which obligations remain unmet, the publisher has no clear way to comply, and the public has no way to judge whether compliance is even possible. Phrases such as "national interest," "distorted information," and "unbalanced reporting" can describe real regulatory concerns. But they are conclusions, not evidence. If the EMA believes particular reports broke the law, it should name them, cite the exact provisions, publish its findings, and explain how it weighed the publisher's written responses. The public should not be asked to accept a severe restriction on the strength of general descriptions. This is not a request for special treatment for The Reporter. It is a basic rule of good administration. A decision with far-reaching consequences must be reasoned, open to review, and open to scrutiny. Openness would also let the publisher answer the allegations on their merits, instead of leaving the public with two competing claims. The law grants power, but does not end the argument Ethiopia's Media Proclamation No. 1238/2021 , as amended by Proclamation No. 1374/2025 , is the legal framework for the EMA's powers. The amended Article 81(1) lets the Authority suspend or revoke a media provider's license or registration certificate. So the question is not whether the Authority has the power to act. It is whether it used that power in a way that was justified, proportionate, and consistent with the safeguards in the law. The amended Article 73(1) says the Authority may take administrative measures "step by step," as appropriate, when a media provider breaks the Proclamation or the regulations and directives under it. That makes the order and scale of enforcement relevant. The EMA should explain what lesser measures came first, which violations remained unresolved, and why an indefinite halt to operations was judged appropriate. The amended Article 81(2) adds a safeguard. Where a case could end in a refusal to renew, a revocation, a fine, or the cancellation of a program, the media organization must be given 14 working days to submit a written response. Suspension is not on that list, but an indefinite suspension that shuts down a publisher is hard to tell apart from revocation in its effect. The EMA should say whether The Reporter was given that opportunity and how its response was weighed. The amended Article 81(3) gives a grievance route to the Authority's Board within 20 working days, and Article 82(1) allows a petition to the Federal High Court within 30 working days of receiving the Board's decision. A right of appeal means little if the affected party cannot understand the case against it or see enough reasons to challenge it. The law should not be read selectively by either side. The EMA's authority deserves respect, and so do the limits and procedures attached to it. Institutional independence is measured in practice A regulator's independence cannot be proved by its title. It shows in consistent decisions, open procedures, and a willingness to explain how public power is used. The public must be able to see that standards are applied on the basis of evidence and law, not political convenience or the identity of the outlet involved. Independent journalism is not an enemy of the state." That standard has to hold across the whole media landscape, whether an outlet is privately owned, state-affiliated, or seen as close to the government. If enforcement is selective, public confidence weakens. If an independent publisher can be suspended indefinitely after a year of monitoring, the public is entitled to ask whether the same standards are applied to outlets whose coverage favors the authorities or to those accused of broadcasting inflammatory content. The EMA could answer that simply by publishing regular data on complaints received, warnings issued, and sanctions imposed, broken down by type of outlet. Regional standards point the same way. The African Commission's Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa says a public regulator with powers over broadcasting must be independent, protected from political interference, chosen through an open and transparent process, and accountable to the public (Principle 17). It also says media registration should serve administrative purposes only (Principle 12(2)). Under the 2025 amendment, the EMA's Director General is appointed by the House of Peoples' Representatives on the Prime Minister's recommendation ( Article 17(1) ). That alone does not make the Authority partisan, but it makes reasoned, public decisions even more important. And a registration certificate that can be suspended indefinitely, closing a newspaper in effect, is hard to square with the idea that registration is only an administrative step. Freedom of expression protects the public, too Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) protects the right to seek, receive, and impart information and ideas. In General Comment No. 34 , the UN Human Rights Committee explains that any restriction must be set by law and must meet the tests of legitimate aim, necessity, and proportionality. Authorities have to show why a restriction is needed. A broad appeal to the "public interest" is not enough. The Covenant's list of legitimate aims is short: the rights or reputations of others, national security, public order, and public health or morals. Harm to investment, tourism, or diplomacy, which the EMA cited, is not on it. National security is, but the African Declaration requires a real risk of harm and a close causal link between that risk and the expression (Principle 22(5)). Article 9 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights also protects the right to receive information and to express opinions. Together, these guarantees mean that access to information is a right that belongs to the public, not a privilege that can be granted or taken away. What the EMA should now explain To restore public confidence, the EMA should answer four plain questions. Show the evidence . Publish the monitoring findings, name the specific articles or broadcasts considered unlawful, and cite the exact legal provisions. Explain the process . Say what steps came before the decision, what chance the publisher had to respond, and how that response was weighed. Justify the penalty . Explain why an indefinite suspension was necessary and why a lesser measure would not have worked. Open the way back . Say which obligations remain unmet and what objective conditions would let the publisher resume work. The issue is not whether Ethiopia needs media regulation. It does. The issue is whether regulation protects the public interest or becomes a way of narrowing public debate when transparency is missing. Independent journalism is not an enemy of the state. It is how citizens test official claims, question institutions, and make up their own minds. A regulator may have the legal power to act, but power has to be explained. A regulator that demands accountability from the press must be prepared to face accountability itself. ethiopia.summary: On November 2, 2026, Ethiopia's Media Authority (EMA) indefinitely suspended the registration of Media and Communication Center PLC, which publishes the Amharic-language Reporter and the English-language The Reporter. This action raises significant concerns about accountability and transparency in media regulation. The EMA claims the suspension was due to the publisher's repeated dissemination of distorted and unverified information, but it has not provided specific examples or evidence to support these allegations. Critics, including Human Rights Watch and Reporters Without Borders, argue that the decision reflects a broader crackdown on independent journalism in Ethiopia, particularly following the publication of a critical editorial by The Reporter. The lack of transparency in the EMA's decision-making process undermines public confidence and raises questions about whether the suspension was politically motivated. To restore trust, the EMA must clarify its rationale, provide evidence for its claims, and ensure that media regulations are applied fairly and consistently across all outlets.

ethiopia.title: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis 18 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Once a bustling border town sustained by cross-border commerce, pastoralist livelihoods and closely interconnected communities, Moyale is increasingly being emptied of its civilian population as escalating clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces drive residents from their homes, disrupt economic activity and push tens of thousands across the border into Kenya. The latest escalation was reported on November 16, when fighting intensified throughout the day, leaving numerous residential homes and businesses burned, while thousands more people continued to flee. Residents who spoke to Addis Standard described a town where the sounds of children going to school and merchants arriving for business have largely disappeared, replaced by military deployments, exchanges of heavy gunfire and the fear of further displacement. Accounts provided to Addis Standard by displaced residents, refugees and a Kenyan Member of Parliament representing the Kenyan side of Moyale point to a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation. Families who have crossed into Kenya in search of safety are confronting shortages of food, milk, clean water and adequate shelter, while those who remain or have returned to protect their properties face continuing insecurity. The escalation comes a month after the conflict erupted on October 18, 2026, following territorial disputes over the hoisting of a Somali Regional State flag in Moyale and the fatal shooting of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa . Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines What began as a familiar confrontation in the dually administered border town, quickly degenerated into armed confrontation between Oromia and Somali regional forces. Fullend by intensive media narrative on both sides, the conflict has since evolved into a wider security and humanitarian crisis , with fighting spreading to neighboring districts into Borana Zone, southern Oromia, and its consequences increasingly felt across the Kenyan border. The scale of displacement reflects the growing severity of the crisis. Nearly 50,000 Ethiopians have fled into northern Kenya, particularly Marsabit County, while more than 10,000 Kenyan residents had also been displaced by the spillover violence. The continuing influx has placed additional pressure on host communities and local administrations already struggling to provide emergency assistance. For many displaced families, however, crossing the international boundary has offered neither lasting security nor relief from the consequences of the conflict. It is almost a month since we fled from Moyale, Kebele 02 (Bole). Yet, what we hear from the direction of our neighborhood is still not good news Kule Boru Kule Boru, a mother who fled from Kebele 02 (Bole) in Moyale town with her three children, all under the age of 10, told Addis Standard that nearly a month after leaving her home, she remains trapped in severe uncertainty and increasingly difficult living conditions. The absence of income in Kenya has made it difficult for her to provide for her children. Two of them are struggling with a lack of milk and adequate nutrition, while the others have been forced to discontinue their education. The family also lacks adequate shelter and assistance. "It is almost a month since we fled from Moyale, Kebele 02 (Bole). Yet, what we hear from the direction of our neighborhood is still not good news; every day we hear the sound of gunfire, homes burning, many people we know dying, and the few people who remained in their neighborhoods being displaced," Kule told Addis Standard . Further describing the difficulties confronting her family, she said: "Here in Kenya, we have no jobs at all. Two of my young children are suffering from a lack of milk; the others have been cut off from their education. The lack of suitable shelter and adequate assistance has put us under immense stress, and we live in constant worry about whether our house will be burned down today or tomorrow." Her experience reflects a broader humanitarian emergency among Ethiopian families displaced into Kenya. A November 10 report by Addis Standard found that food shortages were affecting 71% of Ethiopian displaced families in Kenyan Moyale. Local officials have appealed to UN agencies and humanitarian partners for emergency food, shelter, medical supplies, clean water and sanitation support. From the day the war started, we fled Moyale carrying our newborn baby who had just come into the world. At first, based on what we had seen in the past, we thought this war would last a week at most Abdi Edin The consequences are particularly acute for children, pregnant and postpartum women, and elderly people, whose vulnerability increases as displacement becomes prolonged and access to basic necessities deteriorates. Abdi Edin, a 25-year-old merchant from the Somali-administered side of Moyale, told Addis Standard that he had been forced to flee twice with his newborn baby and postpartum wife after fighting broke out. His wife had given birth only three weeks before the violence began, and the couple had been married for less than a year. Initially believing the fighting would subside within days, Abdi crossed into Kenya with his family and temporarily settled in Al-Huda. But the insecurity and humanitarian difficulties there soon forced them to move again. "From the day the war started, we fled Moyale carrying our newborn baby who had just come into the world. At first, based on what we had seen in the past, we thought this war would last a week at most; however, because the fighting did not stop, we temporarily settled on the Kenyan side at a place called Al-Huda," Abdi told Addis Standard . The family subsequently faced another displacement after heavy weapons fired from the Ethiopian side reportedly crossed into Kenyan territory, causing damage and further threatening civilians. "We faced many humanitarian challenges at Al-Huda. Furthermore, when heavy artillery fired from the Ethiopian side began crossing the border and causing damage inside Kenya, we were displaced once again for a second time," he said. "In search of lasting safety, we left behind our home and property on the Ethiopian side of Moyale. After keeping my family in a temporary shelter for a while, I took them to Takaba Sub-County. Now, after getting my family to a safe place, I have returned to my home." Although he managed to move his family to a safer location, Abdi said the separation has compounded their hardship. His wife is now caring for their newborn without adequate support, while the family's business and source of income have effectively disappeared. "Moreover, my family is now separated; my wife has no one to help her where she is staying. The business we used to have is gone; we have no other income aside from what we spend out of our own pockets. If this continues, even if peace is restored in the future, our economy has been completely paralyzed," Abdi said. After taking my family to a secure place 200 kilometers away in Yabello, I returned to our neighborhood to protect my house from thieves and other threats Liban Guyo The conflict has also forced residents on the Oromia side to make difficult choices between protecting their families and safeguarding their homes and remaining property. Liban Guyo, another Moyale resident, told Addis Standard that he evacuated his family to Yabello, approximately 200 kilometers away, before returning alone to protect his property from looting and other threats. "After taking my family to a secure place 200 kilometers away in Yabello, I returned to our neighborhood to protect my house from thieves and other threats. Now that I am back, my house, where we used to hear the sound of children, has become completely empty," Liban told Addis Standard . He described a town whose ordinary rhythms of life have been replaced by an atmosphere of fear and militarization. "Our neighborhood has completely changed from what we used to know. Previously, when dawn broke in the morning, you would see children going to school and merchants arriving in town from various places. Now, none of that is visible; all we see are military forces." The deterioration becomes even more pronounced at night, when electricity outages and exchanges of heavy weapons have left residents facing prolonged darkness and insecurity. "In the evening, instead of electric lights, what your eyes see is heavy artillery fire being exchanged from both sides," he said. The accounts of Kule, Abdi and Liban illustrate different dimensions of the same crisis: families forced into repeated displacement, parents separated from their children and spouses, and residents returning to increasingly deserted neighborhoods to protect whatever remains of their livelihoods. Together, they reveal how the conflict is dismantling not only the physical security of Moyale's population but also the social and economic foundations of civilian life. A border economy brought to a standstill The humanitarian consequences are compounded by the disruption of economic activities that have historically sustained Moyale and surrounding communities. The town and the wider Borana borderlands depend heavily on pastoralism, livestock trading and cross-border commerce, with markets and commercial networks connecting communities on both sides of the Ethiopia-Kenya frontier. The fighting has brought livestock markets to a standstill, disrupted the movement of goods and left freight trucks stranded on both sides of the border. A November 11 Addis Standard analysis highlighted how the disruption has driven down livestock prices, undermining the livelihoods of pastoralist communities already exposed to economic and environmental pressures. The interruption of commercial trade has also contributed to shortages and rising prices of basic commodities, including cooking oil, rice and milk. This creates an additional burden for displaced families and host communities, particularly as humanitarian assistance struggles to keep pace with growing needs. The economic damage extends beyond the immediate loss of businesses and property. For pastoralist households, the inability to access markets can mean losing the principal source of income from livestock sales. For merchants, transporters and other small businesses, prolonged insecurity threatens commercial relationships and the capital accumulated over years of trading. Even if fighting subsides, restoring these economic networks will require more than the return of displaced residents. It will depend on the restoration of security, reopening of markets, resumption of cross-border movement and rebuilding of confidence among communities whose livelihoods have been severely disrupted. Kenya faces mounting pressure as violence crosses the border The deteriorating situation has increasingly become a concern for Kenyan authorities , as the conflict's humanitarian and security consequences extend beyond Ethiopia's territory. Professor Guyo Waqo, the Kenyan Member of Parliament representing the Kenyan side of Moyale, told Addis Standard that he was deeply concerned by the displacement of more than 50,000 Ethiopian citizens and the continued daily influx of refugees into Kenya. He said the Kenyan administration was coordinating with higher authorities to accommodate and assist displaced Ethiopians in locations including Oda, Olale, Somare, Al-Huda and Butiye. However, he warned that children and elderly people were particularly affected by shortages of milk and balanced nutrition. He also confirmed that several cases of diarrhea had been reported in the Oda area, which he attributed to rainfall and inadequate access to clean water, although no deaths had been recorded so far. Professor Guyo said he had raised the border crisis as an urgent matter in the Kenyan Parliament a week earlier, emphasizing the need for diplomatic engagement rather than allowing the conflict to further destabilize communities on both sides of the frontier. He acknowledged that the Kenyan government has limited authority to intervene directly in an internal conflict within Ethiopia. However, he said diplomatic pressure should be applied to encourage a resolution, alongside emergency assistance for those displaced by the fighting. The cross-border security implications have already become more serious. Professor Guyo said heavy weapons, including RPGs, fired from the Ethiopian side had killed two people and injured dozens inside Kenya, underscoring the danger of the conflict spilling further into Kenyan territory. The UK government has also warned its citizens against travelling to Moyale and within five kilometers of the border area, citing security concerns and the threat of attacks by Al-Shabaab. Kenyan authorities have deployed military forces to secure the border and prevent armed groups from entering their territory, Professor Guyo said, while reaffirming that Kenya remains prepared to receive Ethiopian refugees. Asked whether the displaced could eventually be relocated to established refugee camps such as Dadaab and Kakuma if the conflict persists, he said the proposal had not yet been discussed and would require consultations among relevant stakeholders. Professor Guyo also raised concerns about the political and ethnic rhetoric surrounding the conflict, alleging that some Kenyan politicians were contributing to tensions through inflammatory public statements. "Moyale town is Borana land; however, it is very suspicious that Kenyan officials and Members of Parliament of Somali descent, such as Ali Roba (Governor/Senator of Mandera) and Farah Maalim (MP for Garissa), are preaching hatred in the media and escalating rhetoric to displace the Borana people. These communities have fought each other for decades; what are they hoping for now?" said Professor Guyo. His remarks highlight that the risk that the ongoing fighting could intersect with existing tensions of ownership dispute in the wider border region, complicating efforts to contain the violence. A wider border insecurity beyond the Moyale conflict The risk of further destabilization is underscored by the overlapping security challenges confronting communities along the Ethiopia-Kenya border. On November 16, a separate attack in Ethiopia's Malkamari area killed at least six people, most of them women and children. Although Kenyan authorities clarified that the attack was unrelated to the Moyale conflict, media coverage and public discourse in Ethiopia have increasingly framed the incident as part of the wider conflict, potentially deepening tensions and reinforcing perceptions of an expanding cross-border confrontation. Kenyan authorities attributed the Malkamari attack to tensions involving the Garre and Degodia clans, stressing that it was distinct from the clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces in Moyale. They nevertheless noted that the perpetrators had taken advantage of the broader insecurity along the border. The distinction is important. While the Moyale conflict is rooted in territorial and political disputes involving regional forces, the wider border environment is characterized by overlapping security challenges, longstanding communal tensions and the movement of armed actors across difficult-to-police areas. The deterioration of security in one location can therefore create opportunities for violence elsewhere, even when the incidents have separate immediate causes. The conflict has also drawn increasing human rights scrutiny. On November 17, the Oromo Liberation Army criticized the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission for what it described as insufficient attention to civilian attacks and violence in areas including Moyale, while investigations have focused on other regions. The criticism adds to growing concerns about civilian protection and accountability as the conflict continues. The cost of a conflict without a political resolution Nearly a month into the fighting, Moyale's deteriorating situation raises broader questions about the ability of the federal government to contain regional disputes before they escalate into prolonged armed confrontations with devastating consequences for civilians. Since Monday, November 16, a third attempt to mediate between the warring factions has stalled, despite efforts involving local elders and federal government intervention, Addis Standard has learned. Meanwhile, the continued displacement of tens of thousands, destruction of homes and businesses, disruption of trade and increasing pressure on neighboring Kenya demonstrate that the consequences of the conflict are no longer confined to the immediate territorial dispute. The longer the fighting continues, the greater the likelihood that the humanitarian emergency will become entrenched and existing communal divisions will deepen. The accounts of residents also reveal the growing distance between the immediate security needs of civilians and the political and military dynamics sustaining the confrontation. While families seek safe shelter, food and the ability to resume ordinary life, neighborhoods remain deserted, businesses are shut and residents who return to protect their properties do so at considerable personal risk. For Kenya, the challenge is increasingly twofold: managing the humanitarian needs of a growing refugee population while preventing further violations of its territorial security. For Ethiopia, the continuing conflict presents an urgent civilian protection and governance challenge, with the need for political engagement becoming more pressing as the fighting spreads and the economic consequences widen. Residents and the Kenyan lawmaker interviewed by Addis Standard called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a lasting resolution through dialogue and diplomacy. For a town increasingly emptied of its civilians, the immediate question is no longer simply when residents can return home, but whether the security, economic and social conditions that once sustained their lives can be restored before the conflict leaves permanent scars on both sides of the border. ethiopia.summary: The escalating conflict in Moyale, Ethiopia, has led to a severe humanitarian crisis as clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces have emptied the once-thriving border town of its civilian population. Since the conflict reignited on October 18, 2026, tens of thousands have fled to Kenya, with reports indicating that nearly 50,000 Ethiopians have crossed the border, exacerbating existing pressures on local resources. Displaced families face dire conditions, including food and water shortages, inadequate shelter, and disrupted education for children. The violence has also crippled the local economy, halting livestock trading and increasing prices for essential goods. Residents describe a town transformed from a vibrant community to a militarized zone, filled with fear and uncertainty. As the conflict continues, both Ethiopian and Kenyan authorities are struggling to address the growing humanitarian needs, highlighting the urgent requirement for international assistance and a resolution to restore peace and stability in the region.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 18, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia’s growing defense capabilities are strengthening the country’s ability to safeguard its national interests and contribute to peace and stability across the region, Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Centre Gezahegn Fekadu said. Speaking exclusively to ENA, Gezahegn said the Ethiopian National Defense Force had significantly enhanced its operational capabilities through organizational reforms, improved weaponry, advanced training and broader capacity-building initiatives, particularly since the reform. He noted that the capabilities developed through domestic efforts had not only strengthened the country’s defense readiness but also enhanced its capacity to protect national interests and contribute to regional security. Gezahegn emphasized that sustaining these achievements requires continued military modernization to effectively respond to evolving security threats and challenges. He stressed that a capable and technologically advanced defense force is essential not only for safeguarding national interests but also for promoting regional stability and creating a peaceful environment in which countries can pursue their development objectives. He further noted that the capabilities built by the Defense Force, together with the sacrifices made in coordination with other security institutions, would play a significant role in protecting Ethiopia’s national interests and advancing peace and stability across the region. Meanwhile, Lieutenant Colonel Aragaw Gebremedhin, Policy and Strategy Affairs Team Leader at the Ethiopian National Defense College, said the Defense Force had continued to modernize in terms of technology, training and personnel strength. He noted that Ethiopia’s long-standing contribution to international peacekeeping, from Korea to various African countries, combined with its growing military capabilities, had strengthened its capacity to support peace and security domestically, in neighboring countries and beyond. Aragaw also called on universities and research institutions to document Ethiopia’s peacekeeping contributions and the development of its military capabilities through research and publications. Such efforts, he said, would help present Ethiopia’s peacekeeping experience and contributions more effectively to the international community. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's enhanced defense capabilities are crucial for both national and regional security, according to Gezahegn Fekadu, Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Centre. He highlighted that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has significantly improved its operational readiness through reforms, advanced training, and better weaponry since recent reforms. These developments not only bolster Ethiopia's defense but also its ability to contribute to regional stability. Gezahegn emphasized the importance of ongoing military modernization to address evolving security threats. Additionally, Lieutenant Colonel Aragaw Gebremedhin from the Ethiopian National Defense College noted that Ethiopia's historical role in international peacekeeping, combined with its growing military capabilities, enhances its capacity to maintain peace domestically and in neighboring regions. He urged academic institutions to document Ethiopia's peacekeeping efforts and military advancements to better showcase its contributions to the international community. Overall, a strong defense force is deemed essential for safeguarding national interests and fostering a peaceful environment for development.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Strengthens Pandemic Preparedness, Health Security, Minister Says - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Strengthens Pandemic Preparedness, Health Security, Minister Says - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Strengthens Pandemic Preparedness, Health Security, Minister Says - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Strengthens Pandemic Preparedness, Health Security, Minister Says 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 18, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia has made significant progress in strengthening its health security and emergency response systems, raising its International Health Regulations (IHR) capacity score from 62 to 70, Minister of Health Dr. Mekdes Daba announced. Speaking at the 21st meeting of the Pandemic Fund Governing Board in Addis Ababa, Dr. Mekdes attributed the progress to a 50-million-USD grant from the Pandemic Fund, complemented by an additional 63 million USD in national co-financing. She said the investment had contributed to improvements in laboratory capacity, with more public health laboratories securing international accreditation and 16 laboratories certified under the country's first national biosafety and biosecurity framework. Antimicrobial resistance surveillance sites have also increased from 26 to 41, enhancing the country's capacity to monitor and respond to emerging public health threats, she noted. Ethiopia has also expanded specimen transportation services from health facilities across seven regions, operationalized its electronic emergency management platform in eight regions and screened more than nine million travelers at border entry points, according to the minister. These interventions have strengthened the country's ability to detect, monitor and respond to public health threats. They have also improved national emergency preparedness through the upgrading of National Emergency Operations Centers, completion of the country's first all-hazard risk assessment and establishment of a national community emergency management framework. Dr. Mekdes said the strengthened systems had enhanced Ethiopia's capacity to manage disease outbreaks, including the successful containment of Marburg virus disease, while preparations were underway to address emerging threats such as Ebola. She also highlighted progress in developing the health workforce, noting that field epidemiology training is now offered across some universities. Ethiopia's National Emergency Team has also become the first civilian team in Africa to receive the highest classification for emergency response, she said. In addition, more than 45,000 health extension workers serve as a critical frontline network, helping detect and respond to disease outbreaks at the community level. Emphasizing the importance of sustaining these achievements, Dr. Mekdes called for continued investment, stronger accountability and closer alignment of international funding with national priorities. She urged development partners to support the retention of trained surveillance officers, laboratory professionals and frontline health workers beyond individual funding cycles, stressing the need to ensure that investments in pandemic preparedness produce lasting results. Speaking on behalf of Agriculture State Minister Fikru Regassa, Melkamu Tadesse said the Ministry of Agriculture had expanded in-service veterinary applied epidemiology training from 79 to 429 trainees, while extending its geographical coverage from 74 to more than 300 districts. He said the expansion had strengthened animal disease detection and surveillance, increasing the completeness of national animal disease reporting from 58 percent to 85.5 percent. The improvement followed refresher training for 3,198 frontline personnel in joint outbreak investigation, risk assessment, surveillance and reporting, he noted. On laboratory capacity, Melkamu said rapid diagnostic testing for priority zoonotic diseases and antimicrobial resistance had been introduced in 17 sub-national laboratories. He also highlighted the designation of the Animal Health Institute's veterinary laboratory as a Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reference center for antimicrobial resistance in 2026, describing it as a significant milestone in strengthening the country's animal health laboratory system. Furthermore, 14 regional One Health coordination platforms have been established and strengthened to facilitate collaboration between animal and human health institutions. He cited joint responses to Marburg virus disease, anthrax, human trypanosomiasis and rabies as practical examples of the benefits of stronger cross-sectoral coordination. Meanwhile, Pandemic Fund Executive Head Priya Basu said Ethiopia had strengthened its emergency response capacity through expanded health emergency management systems and a multidisciplinary roster of trained responders. She said the progress demonstrated the country's efforts to translate preparedness investments into operational capabilities. Referring to Ethiopia's response to last year's Marburg outbreak, Basu said the country had mobilized trained personnel and strengthened surveillance and community engagement, demonstrating how investments in preparedness had supported its response to an actual public health emergency. Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI) Deputy Director General Dr. Melkamu Abte said the institute was building on its century-long public health experience to strengthen its position as a regional center of excellence in public health emergency management, research and national health data management. He highlighted EPHI's ambition to become a World Health Organization (WHO) collaborating center for public health emergency management, building on its regional recognition and the recent WHO classification of its emergency medical team as a Type 1 Fixed Emergency Medical Team. The 21st meeting of the Pandemic Fund Governing Board brings together government representatives, global health institutions and development partners to review investments and implementation progress and discuss strategies to strengthen global pandemic prevention, preparedness and response. Established in 2022 and hosted by the World Bank, with technical leadership from the World Health Organization, the Pandemic Fund provides financing to help low- and middle-income countries strengthen their capacity to prevent, detect and respond to public health emergencies. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is enhancing its pandemic preparedness and health security, as announced by Health Minister Dr. Mekdes Daba during the 21st Pandemic Fund Governing Board meeting. The country has improved its International Health Regulations (IHR) capacity score from 62 to 70, thanks to a $50 million grant from the Pandemic Fund and an additional $63 million in national co-financing. Key advancements include increased laboratory capacity, with more facilities achieving international accreditation, and a rise in antimicrobial resistance surveillance sites from 26 to 41. Ethiopia has also expanded its specimen transportation services and operationalized an electronic emergency management platform across eight regions. The National Emergency Team has become the first civilian team in Africa to achieve the highest emergency response classification. Dr. Mekdes emphasized the need for sustained investment and accountability to ensure lasting results in pandemic preparedness. Additionally, the Ministry of Agriculture has expanded veterinary training, enhancing animal disease detection and reporting capabilities.

ethiopia.title: El Niño, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty, New Report Warns
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: El Niño, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty, New Report Warns - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: El Niño, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty, New Report Warns 18 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Nearly 905,000 additional people in Ethiopia could be pushed into poverty and 2.8 million into undernourishment in 2027 as the effects of a potentially exceptionally strong El Niño converge with higher global fuel prices linked to the Iran war, according to a new analysis by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI). The analysis, published on November 17 by IFPRI researchers Emerta Aragie and Chris Hillbruner, projects that the combined shocks could reduce Ethiopia's gross domestic product (GDP) by between 0.4% and 1.1% below its projected baseline, with an average decline of 0.8%. Agriculture is expected to bear a disproportionate share of the economic damage, with agricultural GDP projected to contract by 2% in the average scenario. The researchers identified El Niño-related agricultural losses as the principal driver of the projected economic slowdown. However, higher global fuel prices associated with disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are also expected to compound pressure on household incomes, purchasing power and food security. Using IFPRI's Rural Investment and Policy Analysis (RIAPA) model, the researchers examined how the overlapping shocks could affect agricultural production, economic growth, household incomes, food prices, poverty and nutrition. Their projections are based on three possible scenarios for the 2026 meher harvest, reflecting varying degrees of rainfall deficits and agricultural productivity losses. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Using the above 2027 economic outlook as a baseline, the model suggests it is El Niño's impacts that are likely to slow Ethiopian economic performance, particularly in agriculture, with reverberating effects on household spending, food security, and nutrition," the researchers said. They cautioned that climate-related projections carry greater uncertainty than those associated with global market prices, particularly in the absence of large-scale crop assessments. The meher harvest, which typically takes place between October and December, accounts for more than 95% of Ethiopia's annual agricultural production, making disruptions to the main rainy season particularly consequential. Under the moderate El Niño scenario, agricultural productivity is projected to decline by 2% nationally, while the mild and severe scenarios envisage reductions of 1% and 3%, respectively. The resulting losses would be concentrated in drought-prone areas, with agricultural production in dry highland areas projected to decline by 9.6% and in dry lowland areas by 6.5%. Moist highland and lowland agricultural systems are expected to experience comparatively smaller effects, underscoring the uneven exposure of Ethiopia's agricultural zones to climate shocks. The analysis further projects that agricultural commodity prices could rise by between 0.3% and 1% under the El Niño scenarios, adding to pressure on household purchasing power. Overall, real household expenditure could decline by an average of 1.9%, with urban households facing a larger reduction of 2.8%, compared with 1.5% among rural households. The researchers measured poverty using the international $3-a-day threshold and classified people consuming less than approximately 1,850 kilocalories per adult equivalent per day as undernourished. "These price and income effects have a significant impact on the population's well-being," they said, warning that the combined shocks could deepen existing vulnerabilities even where the overall economic contraction appears relatively modest. More than 57% of those newly pushed into poverty and approximately 76% of those falling into undernourishment are projected to be in rural areas. While the Iran-related fuel price shock is expected to have comparatively limited effects on agricultural production and national GDP, it is projected to account for approximately 472,000 of the additional people falling into poverty and 699,000 of those becoming undernourished. Recent in-depth Addis Standard analyses, The Hormuz Entanglement and The Fertilizer Paradox , have warned that the unfolding crisis extends far beyond temporary supply shortages. They highlighted the convergence of external shocks and domestic structural weaknesses, arguing that the consequences are no longer confined to the energy and agricultural sectors but constitute a broader national vulnerability, with cascading implications for inflation, food security, economic growth and political stability. The researchers also warned that continued conflict in northern Ethiopia could further exacerbate food insecurity and humanitarian needs, although its specific economic and nutritional impacts remain difficult to quantify. The findings come as Ethiopia faces mounting climate-related risks against a backdrop of persistent insecurity, displacement and high food prices. The World Food Program's September 2026 country brief identified food inflation of approximately 15%, alongside insecurity and climate shocks, as factors continuing to erode household resilience. As part of its El Niño coverage , Addis Standard has previously reported on the contrasting drought and flood risks associated with the anticipated exceptionally strong El Niño, including threats to agricultural production in northern and eastern Ethiopia and potential flooding in southern parts of the country. In response, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) appealed for $50 million to assist 4.66 million people across 114 priority woredas between June 2026 and March 2027. The proposed interventions target drought-affected communities in Afar, Amhara, northern Somali and Tigray regions, and include livestock protection, agricultural inputs and emergency cash assistance. Humanitarian agencies have also emphasized anticipatory action, including rehabilitating water infrastructure, strengthening early-warning systems and preparing communities for potential flooding and waterborne disease outbreaks as the October-December rains unfold. IFPRI said Ethiopia's existing social protection mechanisms, particularly the Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), could help cushion some of the effects. However, its projections already account for the food and cash transfers typically provided through the program, suggesting that additional assistance may be necessary to prevent further deterioration in household welfare. The researchers warned that emergency food assistance needs could peak between June and August 2027, making advance planning and resource mobilization essential, particularly amid reductions in humanitarian contributions from key donors. They stressed that the projections are not definitive forecasts but scenarios intended to inform early intervention. The eventual scale of the impact will depend on rainfall distribution, harvest performance, the geographical concentration of crop losses and the evolution of ongoing conflicts. The analysis predicts a GDP decline of 0.4% to 1.1%, with agriculture suffering the most, particularly in drought-prone areas. The report highlights that agricultural productivity could drop by 2% under moderate El Niño conditions, exacerbating food insecurity and household income pressures. Urban households are expected to experience a more significant decline in real expenditure compared to rural ones. The researchers emphasize the need for anticipatory action and additional assistance to mitigate these impacts, as existing social protection mechanisms may not be sufficient. The findings underscore the broader vulnerabilities facing Ethiopia amid ongoing conflicts and climate-related risks.

ethiopia.title: All of Africa Today - November 18, 2026
ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 18, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - November 18, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 18 November 2026 allAfrica.com press review By Melody Chironda South Africa Reprimands Nigerian Envoy Femi Fani-Kayode Over Broadcast Dispute South Africa has formally reprimanded Nigeria's new High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, following a public dispute with the Presidency over the broadcasting of his credentials ceremony. The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) summoned him, with Director-General Zane Dangor reminding him to raise diplomatic concerns through the relevant foreign ministries rather than directly with the president. Fani-Kayode had accused the Presidency of deliberately excluding his introduction and speech from an SABC livestream, a claim disputed by President Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya. The Presidency maintained that Ramaphosa had simply directed the commissioner to raise his concerns with the appropriate SABC official. DIRCO said diplomats are required under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations to conduct official business through foreign ministries. The incident comes amid already strained relations between the two countries over allegations of xenophobic attacks and deaths of Nigerian nationals in South Africa. Ugandan Politician Besigye's Wife Renews Calls for His Release Over Health Fears Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The wife of detained Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye, Winnie Byanyima, has renewed calls for his release, citing serious concerns about his deteriorating health and need for specialised medical treatment. Besigye was arrested in Kenya's capital, Nairobi. He was abducted and taken to Uganda, where he was first charged with treason before his case was transferred to the civilian justice system. Byanyima said that he is experiencing difficulties walking, speaking, and using his hands. His family remains concerned about inadequate medical care under military surveillance. She said that soldiers remain stationed inside and around the hospital room where he is being held, raising further concerns about his welfare. His defence team has also questioned his fitness to stand trial. They argued that his communication difficulties prevent him from properly participating in his defence. Four bail applications have reportedly been rejected, while another is awaiting a hearing date. His next court hearing is scheduled for 25 November. UN Says Over 2,230 Civilians Killed in Sudan Conflict Since January At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 in drone strikes, according to the UN Human Rights Office. Its latest report highlights the growing use of drones by warring parties, with attacks targeting markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities and other essential infrastructure. The Kordofan region recorded more than two-thirds of verified civilian deaths. Attacks on electricity and fuel infrastructure have disrupted healthcare, water supplies and food production. During the first half of the year, the UN documented at least 39 drone strikes on markets, 20 attacks on civilian vehicles and 16 strikes on healthcare facilities. It warned that the actual death toll is likely considerably higher because its figures include only verified cases. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said the violations could amount to war crimes and called for accountability and greater protection of civilians. Guinea Jails 224 Over Illegal Gold Mining A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people, including 22 former regional administrators and 202 alleged illegal gold miners, over unauthorised mining activities in the northeastern Siguiri region. The former officials received two-year prison sentences. The miners were sentenced to three years for offences including environmental destruction, water pollution and illegal mining. Foreign nationals among those convicted were also banned from Guinea for 10 years. The sentences form part of a wider government crackdown aimed at protecting farmland, rivers and the environment from damage caused by illegal mining. The operation has triggered violent clashes between protesters and security forces, leaving 10 people dead and 13 injured. More than 1,200 artisanal miners have been arrested in November. Thousands have fled across the border into Mali, with many awaiting transportation back to their home countries, including Burkina Faso. Ethiopia-Eritrea Fighting Reignites, Raising Fears of Wider War Fighting has resumed along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, raising fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa as relations between the neighbours continue to deteriorate. Ethiopian government forces have pushed Tigrayan fighters to the Eritrean border, with reports of skirmishes and artillery fire near the contested town of Badme. Tensions have also been heightened by Ethiopia's repeated demands for access to the Red Sea, including references to Eritrea's Assab port. The town of Badme remains a sensitive territorial issue between the two countries, even with a peace agreement that awarded the town to Eritrea after their war from 1998-2000. Relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have deteriorated at the same time amid accusations of interference in each other's conflicts, including claims by Sudan that Ethiopia is backing Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, which Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates deny. Analysts warn that proxy involvement could intensify, although direct military confrontation between Ethiopia and Sudan is considered less likely for now. Mozambican Opposition Leader Venâncio Mondlane Goes on Trial Over Post-Election Unrest Mozambican opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial at the Supreme Court over charges including terrorism-related offences, incitement and civil disobedience linked to deadly protests following the disputed 2024 elections. Mondlane, who denies wrongdoing, maintains that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency after he challenged the victory of ruling Frelimo party candidate Daniel Chapo. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging unrest that resulted in deaths, property damage and disruption of public services. He faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge. The trial has prompted tight security in Maputo, with police urging citizens to remain calm and avoid actions that could threaten public order. Access to the proceedings has been restricted to selected media organisations, while live broadcasts have been banned over concerns about possible unrest. The case is widely viewed as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after the disputed elections triggered one of the country's deadliest post-election crises. South Africa reprimanded Nigeria's High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, over a dispute regarding the broadcasting of his credentials ceremony, emphasizing the need for diplomatic communication through proper channels. In Uganda, Winnie Byanyima called for the release of her husband, opposition leader Kizza Besigye, citing serious health concerns while he remains detained. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Clashes Raise Fears of Regional War
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Clashes Raise Fears of Regional War - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Clashes Raise Fears of Regional War © RFI/Noé Hochet-Bodin 17 November 2026 Deutsche Welle (Bonn) By David Ehl As Ethiopian troops push Tigrayan forces toward the Eritrean border, fears of a new regional war are growing. With tensions rising between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, the Horn of Africa faces uncertain times ahead. After a few weeks of relative stability , fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border area have raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have hit new lows. Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23 . It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia . Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme. While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War. The war ended with the Algiers Agreement , in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea , a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles. "It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said. He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region. The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea "The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time ", Abdurahman Sayed said. Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forces during the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties . At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray . Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces. "So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW. However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time." Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab , by force. Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further. Sudan and Egypt , both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD) . The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt . Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF ) , led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti . In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts. Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now. "The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said. Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation. "The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved." ethiopia.summary: Clashes along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border have intensified fears of a potential regional war, as Ethiopian troops advance against Tigrayan forces near Eritrea. Following a period of relative calm, renewed fighting in the contested border area has escalated tensions among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Sudan. The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), supported by pro-government militias, have been pushing the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) out of Tigray since September. The strategic town of Badme, historically significant due to its role in the Eritrean-Ethiopian War, is now a focal point of conflict. Analysts suggest that Ethiopia may aim to reclaim Badme to stabilize its internal situation. Meanwhile, relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have deteriorated, particularly concerning the Grand Renaissance Dam, which has raised water security concerns for Sudan and Egypt. The ongoing civil war in Sudan complicates the regional dynamics, with fears of proxy conflicts rather than direct military engagement for now.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia’s Future Should be Constructed on Sovereign Seaport: Queen’s University Belfast Lecturer - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Future Should be Constructed on Sovereign Seaport: Queen’s University Belfast Lecturer - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Future Should be Constructed on Sovereign Seaport: Queen’s University Belfast Lecturer - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Future Should be Constructed on Sovereign Seaport: Queen’s University Belfast Lecturer 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 17, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia’s maritime future should be built on sovereign ownership of a Red Sea port, not reliance on access granted by its neighbours, Queen’s University Belfast political scientist Bizuneh Yimenu said. According to him, restoring Ethiopia’s coastal status could strengthen the country’s security and economy while opening new possibilities for cooperation across the Horn of Africa. The lecturer in Comparative Politics at Queen’s University Belfast views the loss of Ethiopia’s coastline following Eritrea’s independence in 1993 as a major geopolitical shift, with consequences that continue to affect Ethiopia’s long-term strategic interests. In his view, the process that led to Eritrea’s independence should have included separate negotiations on Ethiopia’s maritime position and unresolved border issues. “The legitimacy of Eritrea’s self-determination and the responsibility of Ethiopian leaders to safeguard Ethiopian strategic interests are two distinct issues,” Bizuneh Yimenu said. The lecturer blamed the transitional government that facilitated the 1993 independence referendum without securing the country’s Red Sea foothold. He believes the issue should now be addressed through diplomacy and political negotiation, rather than rigid legal or constitutional arguments. “The issue should be handled politically in terms of geopolitical scenarios, in terms of regional integration, and from [a] political negotiation point of view,” he stressed. For a rapidly industrializing country with a large and growing population, direct maritime connectivity is vital as approximately 95 percent of Ethiopia’s import-export trade currently moves through a single corridor in Djibouti, Bizuneh elaborated. This concentration leaves Ethiopia exposed to economic and strategic risks, he warned. The scholar sees Ethiopia’s proximity to the Red Sea, alongside its economic and military weight, as giving the country an important role in maritime security. “Ethiopia cannot sit idly when a lot of things are going on in the Red Sea,” he said, adding that the government has a duty to protect its citizens and national interests. Despite the history of tension between Ethiopia and Eritrea, he regards Assab as a potential source of mutual benefit. Ethiopian use of the port could bring Eritrea revenue, jobs and investment, while giving Ethiopia a vital trade route. Closer economic ties could also create shared interests and reduce the risk of conflict between the countries, Bizuneh stated. “There is one theory: countries that trade with each other do not fight each other,” he noted. Looking ahead, he called for a more integrated Horn of Africa, with shared port infrastructure, connected transport corridors and the freer movement of goods and labor. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's future maritime strategy should focus on establishing sovereign control over a Red Sea port, according to Bizuneh Yimenu, a political scientist at Queen’s University Belfast. He argues that regaining coastal access, lost after Eritrea's independence in 1993, is crucial for enhancing Ethiopia's security and economic prospects. Yimenu criticizes the transitional government for not negotiating Ethiopia's maritime rights during Eritrea's independence, suggesting that current discussions should prioritize diplomatic and political negotiations over rigid legal frameworks. He emphasizes the importance of direct maritime connectivity for Ethiopia, as 95% of its trade currently relies on a single corridor through Djibouti, posing significant economic risks. Yimenu sees potential in the Assab port, advocating for closer economic ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea to foster mutual benefits and reduce conflict risks. He envisions a more integrated Horn of Africa with shared infrastructure and improved trade relations, which could promote regional stability and cooperation.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Calls for Scaled-Up, Accessible Climate Finance for Developing Countries
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Calls for Scaled-Up, Accessible Climate Finance for Developing Countries - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Calls for Scaled-Up, Accessible Climate Finance for Developing Countries 17 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Foreign Affairs Minister and COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos has called for climate finance to be mobilized at the scale required, through accessible channels and in line with the priorities of developing countries. Speaking at the high-level session "From Ambition to Action: Mobilizing Finance through the Global Environment Facility (GEF), Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF) and Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF)" at COP31, the Ethiopian Foreign Minister underscored that access to finance and technology is essential for developing countries to translate their national climate ambitions into action. He noted that when resources fall short, the implementation of climate commitments is delayed, vulnerabilities deepen, and confidence in collective efforts is weakened. The Minister welcomed the resource mobilization drive launched to support the strong capitalization of the GEF family of funds, including the LDCF and SCCF. FM Gedion also reaffirmed Ethiopia's readiness to work with all partners to advance climate finance mobilization as the country prepares to host COP32 in Addis Ababa. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's Foreign Affairs Minister and COP32 President-Designate, Gedion Timothewos, has emphasized the urgent need for scaled-up and accessible climate finance for developing countries. Speaking at COP31, he highlighted that adequate access to finance and technology is crucial for these nations to implement their climate commitments effectively. Timothewos pointed out that insufficient resources can delay climate action, exacerbate vulnerabilities, and undermine confidence in global efforts. He welcomed the initiative aimed at enhancing the capitalization of the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and its associated funds, including the Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF) and the Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF). As Ethiopia prepares to host COP32 in Addis Ababa, the Minister reaffirmed the country's commitment to collaborating with partners to mobilize climate finance, ensuring that the priorities of developing nations are met.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Somalia Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 18 - 24 Nov 2026 Format Situation Report Source FAO Posted 19 Nov 2026 Originally published 18 Nov 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 5.18 MB) Review Summary: Significant local rains in the south, little rain in the centre and north. During 10–16 November, Bualle recorded 159.9 mm, Balcad 115.0 mm and Awdheegle 88.4 mm, while most stations in Bay, Hiraan and the centre recorded little or no rain. In the north, Las Dacawo recorded 50.0 mm and Elafweyn 31.5 mm. Satellite estimates (IMERG, 11–17 November) indicate 30–55 mm over Lower Juba and parts of Middle Juba and Gedo. By 16 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%), Awdheegle (265.2 mm, 169%) and Bualle (240.9 mm, 148%), which passed its normal this week. Borama (16%), Burao (21%), Luuq (25%) and Mogadishu (27%) remain far below normal. River levels are rising slightly on the upper Shabelle and the Juba but remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne rose from 2.90 m on 15 November to 3.76 m today, 2.74 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Jowhar (2.90 m) and Bulo Burti (2.30 m) are falling, and Dollow (2.86 m) and Luuq (2.78 m) are rising slowly. Flood water in Jowhar district is receding. Satellite images show about 55 km² of flood water in Jowhar district, down from about 87 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (5–11 November) reported flash floods that drowned livestock at Garadag in Sanaag and a death in stagnant flood water in Hirshabelle, while many callers in the south and centre welcomed the rains and said they had not seen the floods mentioned in the alerts.
