somalia.title: Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain - Al Jazeera
somalia.content: Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain | Politics News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Middle East Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Explained Sport Opinion Video Interactives More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left US-Israel war on Iran Yemen conflict Middle East Africa Asia Asia Pacific Europe Latin America US & Canada caret-right News | Politics Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain President Mohamud’s reforms promise stronger government, but regional resistance and violence threaten the fragile deal of 2012. Listen Listen (11 mins) Save Share Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud addresses an emergency joint session of parliament in Mogadishu [Handout/Somali Presidency] By Faisal Ali Published On 19 Nov 2026 19 Nov 2026 Mogadishu, Somalia – A day before Somalia ’s Supreme Court was due to rule on whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had lawfully extended his term by a year, he abruptly dismissed the chief justice presiding over the case. On November 4, the presidency removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. Five judges proceeded with the case the following day, ruling that constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not apply retrospectively to those already in office. Their mandates, the judges said, had expired. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 ‘Boxed through my skin’: British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali wins first title list 2 of 3 Security forces seized top court, Somalia’s ex-chief justice says list 3 of 3 Somalia’s decades-long journey to stability end of list The government rejected the ruling and immediately swore in a replacement chief justice, setting up a direct confrontation between the president and the country’s highest court over the end of his mandate and the timing of elections. The standoff marks the latest escalation in a two-year political contest over Mohamud’s proposed constitutional changes. Intended to address long-standing structural problems that have hindered Somalia’s reconstruction, the changes have instead deepened divisions over the country’s political future, the nature of its federal system and the distribution of power. Mohamud and his allies believe stronger national institutions, clearer rules and direct elections will help advance Somalia’s decades-long state-building project. The deadlock has increasingly spilled beyond parliament and political negotiations, with tensions playing out on the ground. Advertisement Two federal states have suspended cooperation with Mogadishu, while disputes elsewhere have turned violent. In June, clashes between government forces and militias guarding a former president and prime minister brought part of the capital to a standstill for two days. A federal bargain left unfinished Somalia’s effort to rebuild a functioning national government is one of the world’s longest-running state-building efforts, hampered by a decades-long civil war. After the central government collapsed in 1991, regional administrations emerged around clan alliances, building their own institutions, security forces and revenue streams. Somaliland was the first to emerge from the ashes of Somalia’s civil war, declaring independence in 1991. Puntland followed in 1998, establishing an autonomous administration. Other regional administrations emerged in subsequent years, eventually forming part of the country’s evolving federal system. The provisional constitution adopted in 2012 established a federal framework for sharing power between Mogadishu and the regions. However, some of the most contentious questions over the division of powers and control of resources were deferred as national institutions took shape. Those unresolved questions made governance dependent on constant negotiation. Elections depended on agreements among regional leaders and clan elders, while disputes over power and revenue repeatedly delayed national decisions in the absence of consensus. “Control of ports and trade routes, and relationships with foreign governments, gave some considerable independence from Mogadishu,” Jethro Norman, a Somalia expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera. Norman said Mohamud’s overhaul seeks to give Mogadishu greater legal authority over areas that regional administrations have long controlled, although enforcing that authority is another matter. The seven federal member states of Somalia (Al Jazeera) “What you’re seeing is the federal system crystallising into two camps,” he told Al Jazeera. “You have Villa Somalia presenting the constitution as completing the state: one person, one vote, multi-party politics, democracy, central federal control over foreign relations and national security, and so on.” Puntland and Jubaland, by contrast, see the changes as an imposition that undermines the original federal bargain. “Their view is that the 2012 constitution was a bargain between the centre and the regions, and it can’t just be re-written through a parliamentary majority in Mogadishu when the regions have rejected it,” Norman said. Advertisement Some federal states retain close commercial and security ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which Mohamud, who has frosty ties with Abu Dhabi , has accused of supporting regional leaders in their disputes with Mogadishu. In January, Mohamud’s government announced the cancellation of the UAE’s port and security agreements across Somalia. The regional states, however, rejected the decision. The dispute has added to tensions over the future of the federation. Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni, whose administration is among Somalia’s most autonomous, has even suggested that the country may need to reconsider how it holds together. “If a solution is not found for the current debate, Somalis must deliberate and decide on another alternative way to live together,” he warned. The stakes have also grown with international recognition of Somaliland. Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise the breakaway northern region at the end of 2025. Somali academic Afyare Elmi told Al Jazeera that the government was weakening the fragile consensus underpinning the 2012 settlement by pushing through constitutional changes it could not enforce in states that opposed them. “This is one of the most dangerous times the Somali political system has faced,” he said. “Somalis are no longer moving in the same direction on the future of the state.” Completing the constitution Mohamud himself helped shape the federal system he is now seeking to overhaul. During his first presidency, from 2012 to 2017, his government participated in negotiations to establish or consolidate several federal member states. After returning to office in 2022, he oversaw the creation of another state and made completing the constitution and introducing direct elections key priorities. Yet the boundaries of some federal states remain disputed, reflecting what Elmi, the Somali academic, described as the haphazard way in which the federal system was assembled. Parliament passed the first constitutional amendments in 2024 and approved the remaining changes in March 2026, bringing a 14-year review process to a close. The overhaul seeks to resolve questions about the division of powers that Somalia’s leaders left unsettled in 2012. The changes give Mogadishu greater authority over revenue collection and sharing, elections and the conditions under which the federal government can intervene in member states. They also provide for citizens to elect members of the federal lower house directly through a national electoral commission, although parliament will continue to choose the president. Though Mohamud helped establish several federal member states during his first presidency, Elmi questioned whether he had ever intended for them to exercise significant autonomy from Mogadishu. “Hassan Sheikh always wanted a Mogadishu-centred federal state, with no real federal substance,” he said. Ali Mohamed Omar, Somalia’s state minister for foreign affairs, told Al Jazeera that the previous system, under which clan elders and delegates selected members of parliament, had left successive governments without the public legitimacy they needed. Retaining parliament’s power to elect the president, rather than introducing a direct presidential vote, was a compromise intended to secure the support of some opposition groups, Omar said. Advertisement Mohamed Ibrahim Moalimuu, a federal lawmaker who supports the overhaul, described the president’s decision to press ahead as “daring”. Successive governments had tried and failed to complete the constitution, he said, while most Somalis had yet to gain the right to elect their national representatives directly. “Somalia cannot just remain stuck just because the changes made aren’t considered perfect for everyone,” he told Al Jazeera. For regional presidents and clan elders, however, the changes threaten to diminish their influence over the selection of members of parliament and weaken the political leverage they have built up in negotiations with Mogadishu. Puntland rejected the first amendments in 2024 and withdrew its cooperation with the federal government. Jubaland followed after a dispute over electoral legislation. Both have their own security forces and revenue sources, and their leaders argue that agreements reached without their participation cannot be imposed on them. Elections and political power The consequences have been most pronounced in South West state, where a dispute over President Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen’s re-election in March has escalated into a struggle for control of Baidoa, the regional capital. Mogadishu rejected the vote and federal troops ousted him. Since then, forces loyal to Laftagareen have seized several strategic towns around the city and clashed with government troops. Following Laftagareen’s removal, South West held Somalia’s first direct election for a federal state assembly in May, a milestone for Mohamud’s reforms. The newly elected lawmakers chose Mohamud ally Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe as regional president the following month. Laftagareen, now in exile in Nairobi alongside senior members of his former administration, told Al Jazeera he intended to return to Baidoa and remove Madobe’s government from power. He said he had repeatedly warned Mohamud against changing the constitution without first building broader consensus among the country’s political elite. “Separating powers between the centre and the regional governments saved and kept Somalia together, and making these changes is driving the country apart,” he said. Not all federal states oppose Mohamud’s reforms. His allies now lead four of Somalia’s six states, where recent elections have also strengthened his Justice and Solidarity Party. But the outcome in Hirshabelle, one of those states, has prompted further resistance in its Hiiraan region, where political leaders and elders say long-standing grievances over political representation have yet to be addressed. Armed fighters have occupied parts of the regional administration’s offices in Beledweyne. Moalimuu acknowledged that the recent elections “weren’t totally free and fair”, but argued that giving citizens the opportunity to vote was an important first step. The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, followed by parliament’s election of the president on May 15. The timetable is based on the new five-year terms, even though the Supreme Court ruled that the extension could not apply to officials already in office. Mohamed Mahmoud Dirie, a spokesperson for the Somali Future Council, a coalition of politicians including former presidents and prime ministers, said the group had rejected Mohamud’s invitation to talks in November. “Our request for a guarantor from the international community for whatever is agreed was rejected, which will make it difficult to ensure that the government holds to its side of the bargain,” Dirie said. Advertisement The political divisions are deepening as international support for Somalia’s reconstruction comes under growing pressure. The UN political mission, which supported Somalia’s constitutional negotiations, elections and reconciliation efforts, closed in October at the government’s request. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which is supporting Somali forces in their fight against al-Shabab, also faces funding shortages and uncertainty over continued UN logistical support for its operations. Uganda has begun withdrawing its bilateral troops and plans to withdraw its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, while humanitarian aid is also shrinking. “Somalia is going through multiple difficult transitions,” Mahad Wasuge, executive director of the Mogadishu-based think tank Somali Public Agenda, told Al Jazeera. Wasuge said these changes could leave Somalia increasingly exposed at a time when “the trust between elites is low”. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network
somalia.summary: Somalia's ongoing constitutional overhaul, led by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, is testing the fragile federal arrangement established in 2012. The president's recent dismissal of the chief justice amid a legal dispute over his term extension has intensified tensions between the government and the judiciary. Proposed amendments aim to strengthen national institutions and clarify power distribution, but they have sparked resistance from regional states like Puntland and Jubaland, which view the changes as undermining their autonomy. The political landscape is further complicated by violent clashes and disputes over elections, particularly in the South West state. While some regions support Mohamud's reforms, others argue that they threaten the delicate balance of power that has kept Somalia united. Experts warn that the push for a centralized federal system could exacerbate divisions and lead to further instability, as unresolved issues from the original federal bargain continue to hinder governance and cooperation among the states.

somalia.title: UAE Adviser Calls Mohamud’s Speech an “Attack,” But Doesn’t Address the Allegations - www.ftlsomalia.com
somalia.content: UAE Adviser Calls Mohamud's Speech an "Attack," But Doesn't Address the Allegations - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide UAE Adviser Calls Mohamud’s Speech an “Attack,” But Doesn’t Address the Allegations November 19, 2026 5 min read ABU DHABI , A senior Emirati official has hit back at President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s televised address accusing the UAE of interference, describing the speech as an “attack” that reflects “the volatility of his positions and policies” and questioning whether the Somali leader is prioritising personal interests over his country’s national interest. Dr Anwar Gargash, Diplomatic Adviser to the UAE President, made the remarks in a post on X on Wednesday, a day after Mohamud laid out a detailed case against Abu Dhabi. “The outgoing Somali president’s attack on the UAE reflects the shifting nature of his positions and policies, and raises questions about his prioritisation of personal calculations over his country’s national interests,” Gargash wrote. Gargash said the UAE had “stood by Somalia and its people during the most difficult of circumstances,” and added that it was “regrettable that internal power struggles in Somalia are being dragged into regional disputes that do not serve the interests of its people or their aspirations for security and stability.” He stressed that the UAE’s “relationship with the Somali people will remain deeper and more enduring than transient political disagreements, personal calculations, or individual political ambitions.” Silence on the Substance What Gargash did not do was address the specific allegations Mohamud raised. The President’s speech set out a detailed case: agreements over the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo signed with regional administrations without federal authority; military bases and forces established outside Somalia’s national command; political and financial support that fuelled internal disputes; a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland; and the use of Somali territory at Berbera in January 2026 to move a militia leader fleeing Yemen without Mogadishu’s consent. On each of these points, the Emirati response was silence. The Somali government did not leave the response unanswered. Within hours, three federal ministers had issued replies in Somali, Arabic and English. Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, in a pointed rejoinder, said that “the blood of innocents is not a commodity to be traded,” a direct challenge to the UAE’s framing of its relationship with Somalia as one of enduring friendship. The Mandate Question The most politically charged element of Gargash’s post was his reference to Mohamud as the “outgoing” president. That framing aligns the UAE with the opposition’s position that Mohamud’s mandate expired when the Supreme Court ruled in November that the term extension was unlawful, as detailed in the coverage of the ruling . The government’s position, articulated by the Ministry of Justice, is that the removal of the Chief Justice and the continuation of the President’s term are matters of a transitional constitutional framework that the courts have not settled. For Abu Dhabi to describe Mohamud as “outgoing” is to take a side in Somalia’s constitutional crisis. It is a diplomatic intervention in domestic politics that goes beyond the dispute over ports and bases, and it is likely to harden the government’s position rather than soften it. Critical Note The exchange between Villa Somalia and Abu Dhabi is a battle of narratives, and neither side has emerged with its credibility intact. Gargash’s response was a masterclass in deflection. It attacked the messenger, questioned his motives, and invoked the language of enduring friendship, but it did not engage with a single specific allegation. The ports, the bases, the parallel forces, the Berbera incident, the role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland: all of it went unanswered. That silence is not accidental. A detailed rebuttal would require the UAE to explain its relationships with regional administrations that Mogadishu does not control, its military footprint in a country where it claims to be a partner, and its role in a recognition decision that the African Union and the Arab League have rejected. Those are not questions Abu Dhabi wants to answer in public. But the Somali government’s case has its own weaknesses. The President’s speech was delivered at a moment when his own legitimacy is contested, when his government is fighting its judiciary, and when armed mobilisation in Hiiraan has drawn fighters away from the counter-insurgency campaign, as detailed in the coverage of the Hawadle mobilization . A government that cannot control its own territory accusing a foreign power of undermining its sovereignty is a difficult argument to sustain, however accurate the specific allegations may be. The more important question is what comes next. Gargash’s post did not close the door to reconciliation, but it did not open it either. The Somali government has said it is ready for a relationship based on equality and respect. The UAE has said its relationship with the Somali people will outlast political disagreements. Neither side has said what it is prepared to concede to make that relationship functional again. Until one of them does, the dispute will remain where it is: a stalemate conducted through televised speeches and social media posts, while the ports and the bases and the forces that started it all remain exactly where they were. somalia.summary: In response to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's recent speech accusing the UAE of interference in Somalia, Dr. Anwar Gargash, the UAE's Diplomatic Adviser, labeled the address an "attack" and questioned Mohamud's commitment to national interests. Gargash's comments, made on social media, emphasized the UAE's historical support for Somalia, while failing to address the specific allegations raised by Mohamud, which included unauthorized agreements over key ports and military bases. The Somali government quickly countered, with ministers asserting that the UAE's framing of their relationship as one of friendship was misleading. Notably, Gargash referred to Mohamud as the "outgoing" president, aligning with opposition views on the legitimacy of his mandate. This exchange highlights a broader narrative struggle, with both sides remaining entrenched in their positions. The lack of direct engagement on the allegations suggests a stalemate, leaving unresolved tensions regarding Somalia's sovereignty and the UAE's role in the region.

Opinion Opinion When a minister’s foreign passport eclipses Somali dignity Analysis Why Somalia is key to Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea gambit Opinion When Somalia’s battlefield blood becomes political currency Opinion Ethiopia’s Somaliland restraint is driven by fear, not respect Opinion Raid on Ilhan Omar’s home raises questions over Trump’s power World East Africa Middle East Society News Finland blocks aid grants for Somalia over migrant returns News Somali TikToker loses bid to regain refugee status in Germany News US declines to confirm reported withdrawal from Somalia base News US military accused of trapping civilians in Somalia’s floods News Somalia cabinet approves $1.26 billion budget, down nine per cent Search Opinion When a minister’s foreign passport eclipses Somali dignity November 18, 2026 By Ayaan Abdullahi File photo: Somalia’s state minister for foreign affairs Ali Mohamed Omar attends a cabinet meeting in Mogadishu, Somalia, October 30, 2025. (Somalia Today/File) SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp The primary duty of any nation’s foreign ministry is to advance its strategic interests, articulate its policies on the global stage, and, above all, defend the dignity of its people. When a top diplomat abdicates this fundamental responsibility, the nation is forced to ask exactly whom they are serving. This question is now unavoidable following the recent appearance of Somalia’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ali Omar, on Al Jazeera . When asked to address deeply derogatory remarks made by US President Donald Trump—who has previously described Somalia as “filthy, dirty, disgusting” and recently referred to Somali immigrants as “garbage”—the minister did not offer a robust defence of his country or its diaspora. Instead, he offered a diplomatic surrender wrapped in a conflict of interest. “I am also a US citizen. President Trump was elected by American citizens, so he is the president of the United States. I am not going to respond to what he has said,” the minister stated. This response is a staggering misjudgment of diplomatic duty. Regardless of the broader complexities of US–Somalia relations, or the pragmatic need to maintain security and economic ties with Washington, a Somali state minister’s allegiance in an international broadcast must remain undivided. By shielding himself behind his American citizenship to avoid defending Somalis against explicitly anti-Somali rhetoric, the minister relegated his mandate as a representative of the Federal Republic of Somalia to a distant second place. Diplomatic restraint The issue at hand is not whether Mogadishu should needlessly antagonise the administration in Washington. Statecraft requires pragmatism, and navigating the rhetoric of foreign leaders demands tact. Mogadishu has good reason to handle its relationship with Washington carefully, given crucial US military support in the fight against Al-Shabaab. Yet a Somali minister can acknowledge that security cooperation while still objecting when the US president disparages Somalis. In 2025, Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre provided a blueprint for this exact scenario, firmly but professionally dismissing derogatory comments by suggesting it was better for the nation to “simply move on,” while maintaining the dignity of the Somali people. In December 2025, Somalia’s Defence Minister, Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, offered a similar example—thanking the United States for its military support in comments to Reuters while rejecting Trump’s portrayal of Somalis and pointing to their hard work and resilience. Ali Omar’s approach, conversely, was not diplomatic tact; it was an abdication of his post. Invoking his personal status as an American voter to recuse himself from his professional duties as a Somali minister sends a damaging message to the world and to the millions of Somalis who look to their government for representation. Dual citizenship The minister’s comments also fuel a long-simmering domestic debate over dual citizens in the highest echelons of the Somali government. For decades, the Somali diaspora has been an invaluable asset to the nation’s recovery, returning home to invest, rebuild, and serve in public office. The technical expertise and global networks brought by dual nationals have proved crucial to state-building, while their ties overseas help them speak with authority about the communities they know. Omar’s US citizenship gave him a personal connection to many of the people he was asked about, which he could have drawn on to defend them. Yet the unspoken social contract of dual-national public servants is that, when seated at a Somali government desk, their foreign passports are left at the door. If a passport from a donor nation prevents a minister from politely but firmly defending Somalia’s national character on international television, then dual citizenship ceases to be a diplomatic asset and becomes a severe geopolitical liability. Somalia is navigating monumental challenges, from a complex security transition as African Union forces draw down, to tense regional disputes over sovereignty and the Horn of Africa’s maritime borders. To survive in this volatile geopolitical arena, Mogadishu requires envoys who are unequivocally committed to the Somali cause. Omar should now address Somali Americans directly, reject Trump’s remarks in public, and tell them what they can expect from his ministry when their community is publicly demeaned. A nation working tirelessly to project stability, assert its sovereignty, and shed the stigma of state collapse cannot afford to have its top diplomats signal that their foreign allegiances override their national duties. If a government minister feels that his foreign citizenship prevents him from defending the dignity of the Somali people, he must seriously reconsider whether he is fit to hold the office. somalia.title: Somalia Votes Against UN Resolution On Violence Against Women, US And Russia Abstain - Health Policy Watch
somalia.content: Somalia Votes Against UN Resolution On Violence Against Women, US And Russia Abstain - Health Policy Watch Skip to content menu Home About Us Search for: Search for: Antimicrobial Resistance Infectious Diseases Pandemics & Emergencies Non-Communicable Diseases Health, Climate & SDGs Newsletter Search for: Search for: Somalia Votes Against UN Resolution on Violence Against Women, US and Russia Abstain Women's Health 18/11/2026 • Kerry Cullinan Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Print (Opens in new window) Print Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Vote on UN resolution on eliminating violence against women and girls, 17 November 2026. Somalia was the lone country voting against a United Nations (UN) resolution on “intensifying efforts to prevent and eliminate violence against women and girls” on Tuesday, while the United States and Russia were among the six countries that abstained. The resolution urges member states to “take comprehensive and gender-responsive measures” to prevent and eliminate all forms of “violence, intimidation and attacks” against all women and girls, and to address risk factors by implementing legislation and policies. Its definition of violence extends to online and digital technologies, and urges countries to adopt laws and policies to protect women and girls from defamation and hate speech in online spaces. Digital violence Introducing the draft, France stressed the importance of the resolution’s focus on the digital landscape, noting that over half of women in some parts of the world have been affected by online violence. In August, a report from the UN Secretary-General on progress made to eliminate gender-based violence noted that almost 50,000 women and girls were killed by their partners or another family member in 2024. “Technology has extended the continuum of violence against women and girls into the digital sphere, where online harms increasingly function as precursors to and instruments of lethal violence,” noted the report. “Online stalking, digital surveillance and harassment extend coercive control beyond the physical environment,” it added, singling out “GPS tracking, spyware and monitoring applications” which enabled perpetrators to locate victims. The resolution, sponsored by France and the UK, had been the subject of lengthy debate – as has been the case for most UN resolutions concerning women, girls and gender in the past few years. Various member states contested terminology such as “sexual and reproductive health” and “safe abortion”. Argentina, Burkina Faso, Belarus and Cameroon also abstained. Sovereignty opt-out defeated A proposed amendment, which was defeated by , wanted the entire resolution to be subjected to “national sovereignty”. Nine civil society groups warned that this would undermine multilateralism by adding “a general sovereignty caveat” that would undermine “the process, the international human rights framework and the agreements on which this text rests”. “If accepted here, the same approach could be applied to any resolution in the future,” noted the groups, which include Amnesty International, the Center for Reproductive Rights, Human Rights Watch, International Planned Parenthood Federation and the International Service for Human Rights. “This is not how sovereignty has been understood in the human rights system,” they pointed out. “The Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action addressed this question directly: while the significance of national and regional particularities and of various historical, cultural and religious backgrounds must be borne in mind, it is the duty of States, regardless of their political, economic and cultural systems, to promote and protect all human rights.” Other member states sought to remove “non-consensual language”, including references to “multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination,” “intimate partner violence” and “marital rape”. However, several delegations said that the amendments represented “backsliding,” harming the substance of the resolution. ‘Global scourge’ “Every 10 minutes, a woman is killed by her partner or a family member. This is appalling. And it must end,” said the UK , which co-sponsored the resolution . Welcoming the resolution, the European Union at the UN noted : “Gender-related killings are a global scourge. Today’s vote: 175 to 1 marks the international community’s commitment to end violence against women and girls worldwide.” The US explained in a statement that was disappointed to see the “controversial terminology” of ‘sexual and reproductive health’ and ‘safe abortion’ in the resolution. “There is no international ‘right to abortion,’ whether under that name or under other terms like ‘sexual and reproductive health’,” it added. As the resolution has only been approved at the committee level during the 81st session, it still needs to be formally adopted in December by the General Assembly. somalia.summary: On November 17, 2026, Somalia was the only country to vote against a United Nations resolution aimed at intensifying efforts to prevent and eliminate violence against women and girls. The resolution, which received 175 votes in favor, urges member states to adopt comprehensive measures to combat various forms of violence, including digital violence. The United States and Russia abstained from the vote, citing concerns over controversial terminology related to "sexual and reproductive health" and "safe abortion." The resolution emphasizes the need for legislation to protect women from online harassment and violence, reflecting a growing recognition of digital threats. Despite lengthy debates, including discussions on national sovereignty and terminology, the resolution was co-sponsored by France and the UK, highlighting the international community's commitment to addressing gender-based violence. It still requires formal adoption by the General Assembly in December.

Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia UAE’s Gargash rejects Somalia president’s interference claims UAE’s Gargash rejects Somalia president’s interference claims November 18, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A senior Emirati official on Wednesday rejected accusations by Somalia’s president that the United Arab Emirates had interfered in the country’s internal affairs, describing the remarks as a product of shifting positions and domestic political calculations. Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, wrote on X that the “outgoing Somali president’s attack on the UAE reflects the shifting nature of his positions and policies, and raises questions about his prioritisation of personal calculations over his country’s national interests.” “The UAE has stood by Somalia and its people in their darkest hours,” he said, “and we regret that internal power struggles are dragging Somalia into regional disputes that do not serve its people’s interests or their aspirations for security and stability.” He added that the UAE’s relationship with the Somali people “will remain deeper and stronger than fleeting political disputes, personal calculations, and political ambitions.” The comments followed a televised address on Tuesday in which President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of years of interference that he said undermined Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. Mohamud said the UAE had signed port agreements for Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo with regional administrations rather than the Federal Government. He also accused Abu Dhabi of establishing military bases and supporting forces outside the national chain of command, of backing regional administrations in ways that deepened political divisions, of playing a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, and of using Berbera in January to move a Yemeni separatist leader without Mogadishu’s consent. Somalia’s Foreign Ministry later said the government rejected any foreign engagement or parallel security arrangements that bypassed the Federal Government, which it described as the sole authority for the country’s foreign relations. It called on the UAE to conduct all relations with Somalia through the Federal Government and said it would take all necessary lawful measures to protect its sovereignty. The ministry stressed that its concerns targeted UAE government policy, not relations between the two peoples. The dispute intensified in January when Somalia annulled all agreements with the UAE, including those covering the three ports and bilateral security cooperation, and barred Emirati military and cargo aircraft from its airspace. The government cited actions it said undermined national sovereignty and territorial unity. The UAE has long maintained economic and security ties with both Somalia’s Federal Government and regional administrations, including a major DP World investment to develop the Port of Berbera in Somaliland. Abu Dhabi has repeatedly stated its support for Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and stability. Relations have fluctuated before. Somalia severed ties with the UAE in 2018 under a previous president over similar allegations before later restoring contacts. somalia.summary: The UAE's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Anwar Gargash, has dismissed claims made by Somalia's President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud regarding alleged interference by the UAE in Somalia's internal affairs. Gargash emphasized that the UAE's involvement in Somalia is focused on humanitarian aid and development, rather than political interference. He stated that the UAE respects Somalia's sovereignty and is committed to supporting the country's stability and development. The remarks come amid rising tensions between the two nations, with Somalia accusing the UAE of meddling in its political processes. Gargash reiterated the UAE's dedication to fostering a positive relationship with Somalia, highlighting the importance of cooperation in addressing mutual challenges. The UAE has been involved in various initiatives in Somalia, including infrastructure projects and humanitarian assistance, aiming to bolster the nation's recovery and growth.

الممتاز الهلال السوداني المريخ كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' تترقب الجماهير السودانية انطلاق النسخة 31 من مسابقة الدوري السوداني الممتاز لموسم 2026-2027، وسط تحديات كبيرة، في ظل مشاركة قياسية وغير مسبوقة بحضور 33 ناديًا بالمنافسة. وتنطلق المسابقة يوم الأربعاء المقبل، 25 نوفمبر، بمواجهة قوية تجمع الهلال حامل اللقب بنظيره الأهلي مروي على ملعب كريمة الأولمبي ضمن الجولة الأولى. ويواجه اتحاد كرة القدم المحلي صعوبات جسيمة في إنجاح المنافسة، في ظل أزمة متجذرة تتمثل في عدم جاهزية الملاعب المضيفة وعدد من الصعوبات اللوجيستية، بسبب مخلفات الوضع الأمني المضطرب. أندية الدوري السوداني واتحاد الكرة أمام معاناة مضاعفة تعاني أندية الدوري السوداني من تردي حالة الملاعب، بما فيها ملاعب العاصمة الخرطوم، ما تسبب في تعرض اللاعبين لإصابات متكررة كانت مثار شكوى مستمرة بالنسخة الماضية من البطولة. وقد فاقمت الحرب التي اندلعت في منتصف أبريل 2023 من هذه المعاناة بتدمير البنية التحتية الرياضية؛ وهو ما أجبر اتحاد الكرة على تأجيل المنافسة قبل أن يستقر على إقامتها رغم التحديات والروزنامة المزدحمة. اقرأ أيضًا المريخ يغيّر إستراتيجيته بشأن الدوري قبل العودة إلى السودان خطر التأجيل يهدد ديربي الهلال والمريخ بالدوري الرواندي وفي محاولة لتخفيف حدة الأزمة، سعت عدة اتحادات ولائية إلى تأهيل ملاعبها، كما هو الحال في ملعب مدينة كريمة الذي سيستقبل مباريات المجموعة الثانية شمال البلاد. ومع ذلك، لا تزال الملاعب تعاني من ضعف الجاهزية، ما يضع الاتحاد وأندية الدوري أمام تحديات مضاعفة لإنجاح الموسم في ظل الظروف المتاحة، آملين في عودة النشاط تدريجيا، والتمهيد لمرحلة مقبلة تتسم بتجهيزات مبكرة وفق توجه جديد للاتحاد. لا تتوقف المعاناة عند عدم جاهزية الملاعب، بل امتدت لتشمل أندية الدوري السوداني المشاركة في النسخة الجديدة، إذ بدأ عدد كبير منها تحضيراته مؤخرًا، ما سيؤدي إلى ضعف المنافسة في مراحلها الأولى. وباستثناء فريقي المريخ والهلال، واجهت بقية الأندية صعوبات حقيقية في الإعداد بسبب الظروف الاقتصادية الخانقة التي تمر بها البلاد، وهو ما وضع مدرب المنتخب جيمس كواسي أبياه في مأزق لاختيار قائمته، ليضطر إلى الاستعانة بنجوم القطبين، بينما واجه مدربو المنتخبات العمرية أزمة مماثلة. وقد أجبر العدد القياسي للأندية المشاركة في النسخة الجديدة من الدوري السوداني، اتحاد الكرة على تغيير نظام المنافسة لتُقام على مرحلتين؛ حيث تتأهل 8 أندية للمرحلة الختامية التي أُطلق عليها مسمى "دوري النخبة"، وتلعب مبارياتها من دور واحد، ليتوج باللقب الفريق الأكثر حصدًا للنقاط. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق (الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم) وسط حضور جماهيري كبير في ملعب «جذع النخلة» بالبصرة، خرج المنتخب العراقي بتعادل مثير أمام نظيره الإيراني بهدف لمثله، في ختام البطولة الرباعية الدولية التي تُوِّج بلقبها المنتخب الإيراني، في حين حلَّ أصحاب الأرض في المركز الثاني، في وقت فتحت فيه تصريحات رئيس الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم، يونس محمود، الباب أمام التساؤلات بشأن مستقبل المدرب الأسترالي غراهام أرنولد. وكان المنتخب العراقي قد تقدَّم بهدف مبكر سجَّله حسين علي في الدقيقة الأولى، قبل أن يدرك محمد أمين حزباوي التعادل للمنتخب الإيراني في الدقيقة 83، ليرفع الأخير رصيده إلى 4 نقاط ويُتوَّج باللقب، مقابل نقطتين للعراق، الذي سبق أن تعادل مع لبنان في افتتاح البطولة. وتزامنت هذه النتائج مع تقدم المنتخب العراقي مركزاً واحداً في التصنيف الجديد للاتحاد الدولي لكرة القدم (فيفا)، ليحتل المرتبة 62 عالمياً والسادسة آسيوياً، برصيد 1400.66 نقطة. وأبدى أرنولد رضاه عن أداء لاعبيه أمام إيران، مؤكداً أن المنتخب العراقي أثبت قدرته على منافسة أحد أفضل 4 منتخبات في القارة الآسيوية، رغم مشاركة عدد من اللاعبين الشباب الذين لم يخوضوا تحت قيادته سوى حصتين تدريبيَّتين. وقال المدرب الأسترالي، خلال المؤتمر الصحافي عقب المباراة، إن لاعبيه قدَّموا أداءً جيداً أمام منتخب إيراني قوي، وكانوا الأقرب لتحقيق الفوز، مشيراً إلى أن منح الفرصة للعناصر الشابة يمثل جزءاً أساسياً من المشروع الفني الذي يعمل عليه. وشدَّد أرنولد على أن بناء منتخب قادر على مقارعة كبار آسيا يتطلب عملاً يتجاوز مجرد استدعاء اللاعبين إلى المنتخب الأول، موضحاً أن الاستثمار الحقيقي يجب أن يبدأ من منتخبات الفئات العمرية، وفق معايير وأهداف واضحة. وأضاف أن رئيس الاتحاد طلب بناء منتخب للمستقبل، وأن العودة إلى منافسة كبار القارة تتطلب الاهتمام بتطوير اللاعبين الشباب، خصوصاً منتخب تحت 23 عاماً، والعمل على التأهل إلى الألعاب الأولمبية. إيران توجت بالكأس بعد تصدرها فرق البطولة (الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم) واستشهد أرنولد بتجربته السابقة مع المنتخب الأسترالي، وكذلك بتجربة الكرة العراقية مطلع الألفية، عندما تأهل المنتخب الأولمبي إلى «أولمبياد أثينا 2004»، قبل أن يتوَّج المنتخب الأول بلقب كأس آسيا، عاداً أن الاستثمار في الفئات العمرية يمثل الطريق الصحيح لبناء منتخب قوي ومستدام. وفي تشخيصه لأبرز المشكلات الفنية، كشف المدرب الأسترالي عن تقديم تقرير يتعلق بأزمة مركز المهاجم الصريح «رقم 9» في المسابقة المحلية، موضحاً أنه لا يجد مهاجماً محلياً جاهزاً للاختيار، في ظلِّ عدم اكتمال الجاهزية البدنية لميمي، وإصابة علي الحمادي. وأشاد أرنولد بإمكانات اللاعب الشاب أموري فيصل، وكذلك بالمستوى الذي قدَّمه الحارس كميل خلال مباراتين، لكنه أشار إلى أن قلة مشاركة بعض اللاعبين مع أنديتهم تمثل تحدياً أمام الجهاز الفني، خصوصاً فيما يتعلق بجاهزيتهم البدنية للمباريات الدولية. وتطرق إلى وضع حيدر عبد الكريم، مؤكداً أن اللاعب مطالب بمعالجة وضعه بنفسه، بعدما ابتعد عن المشاركة لمدة عامين، مشيراً إلى أن حيدر وداريو نامو لا يشاركان مع نادييهما، وأن اللاعب الذي ينضم إلى المنتخب يجب أن يكون جاهزاً لخوض المباريات الدولية. بدوره، أثار رئيس الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم يونس محمود، التساؤلات بشأن هوية المدرب الذي سيقود المرحلة المقبلة، بعدما أكد أن خيار المدرب المحلي مستبعد من حسابات الاتحاد. وأوضح محمود، في تصريحات نقلتها «وكالة الأنباء العراقية»، أن الاتحاد يبحث عن مدرب من خارج العراق يمتلك القدرة على التعامل مع عقليات اللاعبين المحترفين في الدوريات الأوروبية، مشيراً إلى وجود 15 لاعباً عراقياً ينشطون في أوروبا. وقال إن الاتحاد لا يريد تكرار الأخطاء السابقة في اختيار المدربين، بعدما شهد هذا الملف كثيراً من الجدل، مؤكداً أهمية الوصول إلى توليفة متجانسة يكون فيها اللاعبون مكملين لبعضهم بعضاً. وأشار رئيس الاتحاد إلى أن المدرب القادم قد يكون أرنولد نفسه أو غيره، وأن المعيار الأساسي في الاختيار سيكون القدرة على التعامل مع اللاعبين المحترفين في أوروبا وفهم طبيعة عقلياتهم. مواضيع رياضة كرة القدم العراق عودة الدوليين تشعل تدريبات الأهلي المصري قبل football.summary: تأهل فريقا المغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد تحقيقهما انتصارات مهمة في مباريات الإياب. حيث تمكن المغرب الفاسي من الفوز على أسيك ميموزا العاجي بنتيجة 2-1 في أبيدجان، بعد أن تعادل الفريقان في مباراة الذهاب 1-1. سجل أهداف المغرب الفاسي كريستوفر إيبايي وخالد بابا، الذي أحرز هدف الفوز في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت بدل الضائع. من جهة أخرى، حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مريحاً على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليكرر نتيجة الذهاب. سجل إرنست لوزولو ومحمد عبد الرحمن "الغربال" أهداف الهلال في الشوط الأول. هذا التأهل يعوض الهلال خروج منافسه التقليدي المريخ من البطولة. كما تأهل سيمبا التنزاني وكولومب الكاميروني بعد انتصاراتهما في مبارياتهما.

قصص رياضية الرئيسية / الكرة السعودية السنغال تلامس التأهل برباعية السودان.. ولوبي يصنع نيكولاس جاكسون، مهاجم المنتخب السنغالي، يحتفل وبرفقته الحاج مالك ضيوف، الظهير الأيسر، بعد تسجيل الهدف الأول أمام السودان، الإثنين، ضمن تصفيات أمم إفريقيا (المركز الإعلامي ـ الاتحاد الإفريقي) الرياض ـ الرياضية 2026.11.16 | 06:39 pm اقترب المنتخب السنغالي الأول لكرة القدم من حسم تأهله إلى نهائيات كأس أمم إفريقيا 2027، بفوزه 4ـ2 على مضيفه السوداني، في مباراة جمعتهما، الإثنين، على ملعب مدينة جوبا، عاصمة جنوب السودان، لحساب الجولة الرابعة من عاشر مجموعات التصفيات. وجلس الثلاثي السنغالي خاليدو كوليبالي، مدافع الهلال، وموري دياو، حارس مرمى الشباب، وكلايتون دياندي، جناح الدرعية، على مقاعد البدلاء دون مشاركة، فيما لعب مواطنهم مالانج سار، مدافع نيوم، المباراة كاملة، ودخل زميلهم ديون لوبي، لاعب وسط الاتحاد، بديلًا في الدقيقة 77، وصنع الهدف الثالث بتمريرة طويلة. وتقدم السنغاليون بهدفين سجلهما نيكولاس جاكسون، رأس الحربة، والحاج مالك ضيوف، الظهير الأيسر، في الدقيقتين 4 و22. واستطاع السودان إدراك التعادل عن طريق الجزولي نوح، وصلاح الدين عادل، لاعبي الوسط، في الدقيقتين 52 و75. وفيما كان المنتخب السوداني يبحث عن إكمال العودة والفوز، تلقت شباكه هدفًا سنغاليًا في الدقيقة 87 بتوقيع الجناح باتي مبوب، وتبعه آخر بواسطة المهاجم بول ميندي مع بداية الوقت بدل الضائع، ليحسم «أسود التيرانجا» اللقاء. وتجبر الظروف الراهنة في السودان المنتخب الملقب بـ «صقور الجديان» على اللعب خارج أرضه في مدينة جوبا. ورفع الفوز رصيد السنغال إلى 10 نقاط، وواصلت احتلال الصدارة، أمام موزمبيق صاحبة النقاط الأربع، والسودان وإثيوبيا المتساويتين بثلاث نقاط. وتتواجه موزمبيق مع إثيوبيا، الثلاثاء، لحساب الجولة ذاتها في محاولة لتعزيز حظوظهما في التأهل. وإذا فازت موزمبيق، ستضمن السنغال تأهلها قبل جولتين من النهاية، لاستحالة وصول رصيد إثيوبيا والسودان إلى أكثر من 9 نقاط. تصغير تكبير مشاركة مشاركة تابع آخر أخبار الرياضية على Google football.summary: أمجد قلق هو مهاجم فريق الهلال السوداني، حيث يحمل القميص رقم 36. وُلد في 1 نوفمبر 2003، ويبلغ من العمر 23 عامًا. يُعتبر قلق أحد اللاعبين البارزين في الفريق، حيث يساهم بشكل فعال في المباريات. الهلال السوداني يشارك في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث يتضمن جدول المباريات القادمة عدة مواجهات مهمة، منها مباراة ضد هورويا في 29 نوفمبر 2026، ومباراة أخرى ضد المغرب الفاسي في 4 ديسمبر 2026. كما سيواجه الفريق بيراميدز في 18 ديسمبر 2026. يُظهر أمجد قلق إمكانيات كبيرة في الملعب، مما يجعله لاعبًا محوريًا في تشكيل الفريق. لمزيد من المعلومات حول اللاعب وأخباره، يمكن متابعة الموقع الرسمي الذي يقدم تحديثات مستمرة حول الرياضات والمباريات.

football.summary: انتهت مباراة السودان ضد السنغال في تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية بالتعادل 0-0. أقيمت المباراة في جوبا يوم الإثنين، 16 نوفمبر 2026، حيث لم يتمكن أي من الفريقين من تسجيل الأهداف. كانت المباراة جزءًا من الجولة الرابعة من التصفيات، وقد شهدت أداءً متوازنًا من كلا الفريقين، مع محاولات هجومية ولكن دون جدوى. على الرغم من عدم تسجيل الأهداف، إلا أن المباراة كانت مثيرة، حيث تبادل الفريقان السيطرة على الكرة وخلق الفرص. يُذكر أن هذه المباراة تأتي في إطار سعي السودان للتأهل إلى البطولة الأفريقية، بينما تسعى السنغال للحفاظ على مكانتها كأحد الفرق القوية في القارة. تواصل التصفيات تقديم تحديات كبيرة للفرق المشاركة، مع أهمية كل نقطة في تحديد مصيرها في البطولة.
